Chapter 1: Read This First / Before We Start: The Pro Guide to Learning Jazz Standards

<<<CHAPTER FILE
# Chapter 1 — Read This First / Before We Start: The Pro Guide to Learning Jazz Standards

_Pages 5-20._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. The transcript may contain extraction artifacts where the book's typeface confuses the tool — e.g. `7irst` or `<irst` for `first`, `speci7ic` for `specific`. **Do NOT manually fix these in this file**: the quote-fidelity validator compares against the raw transcript, so a 'fixed' quote will fail verification and break Stage 2 idempotency. If a future pipeline iteration adds artifact-normalization, it must normalize the transcript and these files together.

## Learning jazz by ear vs. sheet music

> Jazz is not music meant to be learned from sheet music. It never was. Back in the bebop days in the 1940's, jazz musicians would pile into clubs and listen to each other play. They would literally pick things up on the bandstand, in rehearsals, and just by listening to records.
>
> That doesn't mean they couldn't read music, or never read music, but learning music by ear was always the primary method. That's something | want you to understand. Jazz is first and foremost aurally learned music. So if you want to become a great jazz improviser, you need to follow in the footsteps of the great jazz musicians before you.

**Significance (p. 10).** This passage establishes the book's foundational methodological rule -- ear-first learning over sheet music -- which governs every subsequent lesson and exercise.

## Sheet music's proper role

> The idea is not to throw away sheet music but to know its place. If you genuinely want to become great jazz improviser, you are going to need to get your face out of the pages and open up your ears instead.

**Significance (p. 11).** This defines the precise, limited role sheet music should play, preventing misapplication of the ear-learning rule and clarifying when referencing notation is acceptable.

## Ear training and harmonic reaction

> This is where sharpening your ear comes in. Let's say you are playing a jazz standard and a ii-V-| chord progression is coming up in the form (in the key of C: Dmin7-G7-Cmaj7).
>
> But suddenly you hear the piano player approach it chromatically (Ebmin7-Ab7-Dmin7-G7-Cmaj7). What do you do? Do you double check the sheet music to see if the piano player is playing the "correct" chord changes, and then scold him or her for getting it wrong? Of course not.
>
> Jazz is not predictable. Sheet music is. When we learn jazz language by ear, we are training ourselves to respond to the music with our ear.

**Significance (p. 12).** This concrete example of a chromatic substitution illustrates why aural training is functionally necessary for real-time improvisation, not just pedagogically preferred.

## The LIST process defined

> In comes my handy little acronym for learning jazz standards and jazz language in general: LIST.
>
> >> THELIST PROCESS:
>
> Listen
> Internalize
> Sing
>
> Transfer

**Significance (p. 14).** This introduces the book's central procedural framework -- the four-step LIST method -- which structures every jazz standard study that follows.

## Listen step: put instrument away

> The most important thing you can do when learning jazz standards is put your instrument away and just listen. Find as many recordings as possible of the jazz standard you want to learn and go through all of them. You need to become acquainted with the song, and without becoming acquainted with it first, you will have started off on the wrong foot.

**Significance (p. 15).** This gives the concrete rule for the Listen step -- instrument away, multiple recordings -- which is a specific behavioral directive, not just general advice.

## Pro Tip: Learn the lyrics

> >> PRO TIP #1: LEARN THE LYRICS
>
> When choosing versions to listen to, always include one with a vocalist if possible. This is obvious to singers, but not always so obvious to instrumentalists.
>
> Learning lyrics is extremely helpful for internalizing melodies. Especially in the case of many jazz standards, they are poetic, memorable, and tell the story and essence of the song.

**Significance (p. 15).** This rule directs instrumentalists to include vocal recordings and learn lyrics as a memory and internalization technique, a non-obvious but method-specific directive.

## Sing step: proving internalization

> The primary application of singing involves the melody. Be sure that you can sing the melody of the standard, both along with the recording and on your own, before you learn it on your instrument.
>
> You may have heard the saying before, "if you can sing it, you can play it."

**Significance (p. 17).** This defines the Sing step's success criterion -- singing alone and with recording before touching the instrument -- making it an actionable gate in the learning sequence.

## Pro Tip: Finding the basic melody

> >> PRO TIP #2: FINDING THE BASIC VERSION OF THE MELODY
>
> One common complaint | get is not knowing what the "correct" melody is because jazz musicians take so many liberties with it. Here's something to remember: Frank Sinatra is your friend. Frank almost always sings melodies straight. So if there is a version of Frank doing it, check it out. Throughout our studies, | do my best to include a Sinatra version when available.
>
> If it's a less classic song, identify the original composer or artist who originally performed it. Chances are, they are going to play the melody true to its original intent.
>
> Do listen to, but avoid learning melodies from artists like Billie Holiday or Miles Davis. They always mess with the melody (unless it's their composition).

**Significance (p. 17).** This gives specific, actionable source-selection rules -- use Sinatra or original composers, avoid Holiday and Davis -- for students trying to identify a reliable reference melody.

## Singing bass notes for harmony

> If you want to take singing a step further, try singing the bass notes. This will help you begin to learn the harmony (chord progressions) of the jazz standard. Listen in to the bass instrument on your recordings
>
> and see if you can sing the roots. This is a more advanced tip, but this will help you along with the next step.

**Significance (p. 18).** This extends the Sing step into harmonic ear training by using bass-note singing as a bridge technique to learning chord progressions by ear before picking up the instrument.

## Transfer step: melody then chords

> 1. Transfer the melody. Start learning the melody on your instrument. Again, this should only be a matter of you taking what you can already sing and finding the notes on your instrument. Once you find the notes, follow through with plenty of repetition so that muscle memory starts kicking in.
>
> 2. Learn the chords. This is the most challenging part of learning songs by ear, but | encourage you to do your best! It is incredibly helpful to have a good understanding of how jazz harmony works.

**Significance (p. 19).** This defines the two-part sequence of the Transfer step -- melody first, then chords -- and identifies chord learning by ear as the hardest stage, setting realistic expectations.

## Pro Tip: Listen to bass notes for chord ID

> >> PRO TIP #3: LISTEN TO THE BASS NOTES
>
> Like | mentioned in the Sing step, the bass note movement is very important. For example, if you can identify that the bass player is playing a concert Eb note for the first chord, then all you have to do is figure out what quality it is. Then you listen to the bass note of the next chord. Let's say the following bass note is a concert C. From there you can start to identify the chordal movement.

**Significance (p. 19).** This provides the concrete two-step technique for learning chord progressions by ear: isolate the bass root first, then determine chord quality -- a practical method, not just a principle.

## Chromatic approach (CA) defined

> CA: stands for "chromatic approach." Represents a non-diatonic note approaching a diatonic note, usually by a half step.

**Significance (p. 7).** This defines a notation symbol used throughout the book's exercises, making it load-bearing for interpreting all subsequent musical examples correctly.

## Chromatic passing (CP) defined

> CP: stands for "chromatic passing." Represents a non-diatonic note that connects two diatonic notes in either half steps or a combination of whole and half steps.

**Significance (p. 7).** This defines a second recurring notation symbol distinct from CA, establishing the specific melodic function of chromatic passing tones used throughout the book's improv examples.
